Amon. The hidden king of the gods and chief deity of ancient Egypt's New Kingdom, though he began as a simple local deity. Originally worshipped as a god of Thebes, modern Luxor, Amon rose to supreme prominence as imperial power consolidated there. He was eventually merged with Ra to form Amon-Ra, combining the hidden creative force with the visible sun god's power, creating the most powerful god in Egypt's entire pantheon. Amon was typically depicted as a ram-headed god with curled horns, though also shown in human form as a king crowned with feathers. He held the title King of the Gods and ruled the divine pantheon from his great temple at Karnak in Thebes. His very name meant "the hidden one," referring to the invisible creative forces and the wind that he represented. He was associated with fertility, sexuality, and the creative breath of existence. The annual Nile flood was attributed to Amon's generosity and power, making him essential to Egypt's agricultural survival and prosperity. Pharaohs styled themselves as the son of Amon, further elevating his status as a divine parent who legitimized their rule and connected them to divine authority. By the late New Kingdom, his priests at Karnak had become so wealthy and politically powerful that they rivaled pharaonic power itself, wielding influence over the state.
